items.followUp: State two assumptions of the kinetic molecular model of matter.

rubric.why: Identifies that matter is made up of tiny particles.
rubric.description: Matter consists of tiny particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that matter is made up of tiny particles.

rubric.why: Gives a second feature of the model: particles are always moving.
rubric.description: Particles are in continuous random motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles are continuously or randomly moving.

modelAnswer: Matter is made up of tiny particles.
These particles are in continuous random motion.

items.followUp: Explain how a submarine can sink and rise in water.

rubric.why: States the usual behaviour of a ship in water.
rubric.description: A ship floats on the surface of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for distinguishing a ship as floating on the water's surface.

rubric.why: Identifies the submarine's ability to submerge or rise, usually by controlling water in its ballast tanks.
rubric.description: A submarine can submerge and rise by controlling water in its ballast tanks.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the submarine's underwater movement or ballast-tank control.

modelAnswer: A ship floats on the surface of water.
A submarine can submerge and rise; it controls its buoyancy by taking water into or expelling water from its ballast tanks.

rubric.why: Identifies the temperature given on the Kelvin scale.
rubric.description: Given temperature is 300 K.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly recording the given temperature.

rubric.why: Uses the Kelvin-to-Celsius conversion and obtains the correct result.
rubric.description: Celsius temperature is 27 °C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct conversion and answer.

modelAnswer: Given: T = 300 K
Formula: t = T − 273
Substitution: t = 300 K − 273
Answer: t = 27 °C

items.followUp: Define the internal energy of a body.

rubric.why: Includes both forms of molecular energy that make up internal energy.
rubric.description: Internal energy is the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning both kinetic energy and potential energy.

rubric.why: Makes clear that these energies belong to the molecules of the body.
rubric.description: The energies are those of the body's molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating the energies to the molecules of the body.

modelAnswer: The internal energy of a body is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules.

items.followUp: Write four differences between distance and displacement.

rubric.why: Distinguishes mass as scalar and weight as vector.
rubric.description: Mass is scalar; weight is vector.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this correct distinction.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the physical meaning of mass and weight.
rubric.description: Mass measures amount of matter; weight is gravitational force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly comparing their meanings.

rubric.why: Gives the correct SI units for both quantities.
rubric.description: Mass is measured in kilograms; weight in newtons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both correct units.

rubric.why: States that mass is location-independent while weight varies with gravitational field strength.
rubric.description: Mass is constant from place to place; weight depends on gravity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this correct comparison.

modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force acting on it.
Mass is a scalar quantity; weight is a vector quantity.
The SI unit of mass is kilogram (kg); the SI unit of weight is newton (N).
Mass remains constant with location; weight changes when gravitational field strength changes.

items.followUp: State and explain the second condition for equilibrium.

rubric.why: States that the total force on a body in equilibrium is zero.
rubric.description: The resultant force acting on the body is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the zero-resultant-force condition.

rubric.why: Explains that the horizontal components of force must balance.
rubric.description: The sum of horizontal force components is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the horizontal component condition.

rubric.why: Explains that the vertical components of force must balance.
rubric.description: The sum of vertical force components is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the vertical component condition.

accept: remains at rest or uniform motion
rubric.why: Connects the condition to the absence of acceleration and translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: The body is in translational equilibrium and has no acceleration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct explanation or consequence.

modelAnswer: First condition for equilibrium: the resultant force acting on a body must be zero.
In symbols: ΣF = 0.
Thus, the horizontal and vertical components of the forces balance: ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
The body is then in translational equilibrium, with no acceleration.

items.followUp: Define base and derived quantities and give one example of each.

accept: cannot be expressed in terms of other quantities
rubric.why: Defines base quantities as independent quantities.
rubric.description: A base quantity is independent and is not defined in terms of other quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition of a base quantity.

rubric.why: Gives a valid base-quantity example.
rubric.description: Example of a base quantity: length, mass or time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example of a base quantity.

accept: expressed in terms of base quantities
rubric.why: Clarifies the distinction between base and derived quantities.
rubric.description: A derived quantity is obtained from base quantities.
rubric.how: This distinction is included in the definition mark; no additional mark is allocated.

rubric.why: Provides possible examples of derived quantities.
rubric.description: Examples of derived quantities include area, speed, volume and density.
rubric.how: This is included as clarification; no additional mark is allocated.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent quantities that are not defined in terms of other quantities; length is an example.
Derived quantities are obtained by combining base quantities; speed is an example.

items.followUp: Estimate the number of seconds in 12 years.

rubric.why: Identifies the time interval to be converted.
rubric.description: Given time is 14 years.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly recording the given time.

rubric.why: Converts years to seconds using the appropriate time-unit conversions.
rubric.description: Uses 365 days per year and converts days to hours, minutes and seconds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct conversion setup or equivalent calculation.

rubric.why: Gives the estimated number of seconds with the correct unit.
rubric.description: Approximately 4.4 × 10⁸ seconds.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct answer with seconds; award 1 mark if the numerical result is correct but the unit is missing.

modelAnswer: Given: t = 14 years
Using 1 year = 365 days, 1 day = 24 h, 1 h = 60 min and 1 min = 60 s
Substitution: t = 441,504,000 s
Answer: t ≈ 4.4 × 10⁸ s
